unitDescription.value: In this unit, students develop an understanding of Australian and Aboriginal histories and cultures while building empathy as a core design skill. Students explore how culture, context, and lived experience influence design decisions, and examine the importance of ethical and respectful design when responding to Aboriginal perspectives. Through guided learning, students consider how designers can create solutions that acknowledge cultural significance, community needs, and social impact. The unit emphasises empathy, reflection, and responsible decision-making, encouraging students to design with awareness of Australia’s cultural diversity and shared histories.

description.value: In this assessment, students complete a designed solution task under exam-style time constraints to simulate working to a real-world deadline. Students are given an Australia-based design scenario and follow the final stages of the design process to generate, revise, evaluate, and refine a solution. Evaluation of the design must explicitly demonstrate empathy skills, including consideration of user perspectives, cultural context, and social impact. This assessment focuses on students’ ability to apply ethical, culturally informed, and reflective thinking to design decisions.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students explain how people consider factors that impact on design decisions and the technologies used to design and produce products, services and environments for sustainable living. They explain the contribution of innovation, enterprise skills and emerging technologies to global preferred futures. For one or more of the technologies contexts, students explain the features of technologies and their appropriateness for purpose, and create designed solutions based on an analysis of needs or opportunities. Students create, adapt and refine design ideas, processes and solutions and justify their decisions against developed design criteria that include sustainability. They communicate design ideas, processes and solutions to a range of audiences, including using digital tools. Students independently and collaboratively develop and apply production and project management plans, adjusting processes when necessary. They select and use technologies skilfully and safely to produce designed solutions.

lessons.title: Introduction to Human-Centred Design and Empathy
lessons.learningGoal: Define core principles of Human-Centred Design and explain the role of empathy in identifying user pain points.

activities.title: HCD Principles Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Model the five iterative stages of Human-Centred Design: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test. Explicitly demonstrate the distinction between designer assumptions and authentic empathy using public infrastructure initiatives from Livingstone Shire Council (https://www.livingstone.qld.gov.au/) as an exemplar. Walk through the layout of the workbook matching table, pointing out that terms are locked on the left and the definition bank below must be matched into the blank column.
activities.studentsDo: Read the locked terms in column 1 of the workbook table and match each term to its exact definition using the definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each Human-Centred Design term in column 1 to its correct definition from the bank provided below the table by writing the matching letter in the blank column.
activities.questioning:
Why is the Empathise stage critical before attempting to Ideate or Prototype? Expected: It ensures designers uncover genuine lived human needs and constraints rather than designing solutions based on their own flawed assumptions.
What does the empathy gap represent when designing civic or school facilities? Expected: The disconnect between what designers assume users experience and the actual physical or social barriers users face daily.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions written out: Empathise: Developing a deep understanding of user needs and experiences through immersion and observation. Define: Synthesising observations into a clear, actionable problem statement. Ideate: Generating a wide range of creative and divergent solution concepts. Prototype: Building rapid, tactile, or visual low-fidelity representations to explore ideas. Test: Engaging real end-users to trial solutions and gather critical feedback.
activities.eLearning: Engage with the visual breakdown of the HCD methodology presented on screen.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students that we will now consolidate these five principles into connected technical notes.

activities.title: Empathy Gap Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to conduct an empathy gap analysis using the Keppel Bay Marina facility (https://www.keppelbaymarina.com.au/) as a case study. Show how a designer might assume 'timber ramps offer scenic access' while a wheelchair user or parent with a double pram experiences steep tidal inclines and slippery wet decking during coastal storms. Demonstrate how to write precise, evidence-based user constraints using the three-section format in the workbook.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the three-part structured written response in the workbook, identifying a specific visitor group at Keppel Bay Marina, their physical or situational pain points, and an empathetic design response.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the three structured sections analysing user constraints and proposing an empathetic design modification for Keppel Bay Marina.
activities.questioning:
What environmental factor at Keppel Bay Marina magnifies physical mobility challenges? Expected: Coastal weather events and fluctuating tides that change ramp gradients and make timber surfaces slippery.
How does designing for people with extreme constraints benefit everyday users? Expected: Accessible, slip-resistant, and gently graded paths improve safety and ease of transit for all marina visitors, including young families and delivery workers.
activities.scaffolding: Sentence starters provided in workbook sections: 'User group and context: ...', 'Observable pain point: ...', 'Empathetic design intervention: ...'. Focus on physical constraints, sensory factors, and environmental conditions.
activities.eLearning: Display the Keppel Bay Marina site imagery on the main screen to provide visual environmental context.
activities.transition: Wrap up the generative writing and prepare for the Culminate summary.

workbookSpec.title: Keppel Bay Marina Empathy Gap Analysis
workbookSpec.prompt: Analyse the user experience constraints at Keppel Bay Marina by completing the structured sections below.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. User group and context: Elderly visitors and individuals using mobility aids navigating gangways to access berthed vessels at Keppel Bay Marina.
2. Observable pain point: Tidal shifts create steep gangway inclines, and wet timber or pontoon surfaces present severe slip hazards and lack continuous grab rails.
3. Empathetic design intervention: Install automated grade-levelling access pontoons with textured marine-grade composite decking and tactile, illuminated handrails.

sections.label: 1. Identify target user group and environmental context
2. Detail the observable user pain point and empathy gap
3. Propose an empathetic, human-centred design intervention

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. User group: Elderly visitors, wheelchair users, or families with prams moving between the marina carpark, boardwalk, and pontoon berths.
2. Pain point: Steep gangway angles during low tide and slippery wet surfaces that restrict safe, unassisted navigation.
3. Design intervention: High-friction non-slip grating, continuous bi-level handrails, and gradual switchback ramp geometry to eliminate steep pinch points.

lessons.title: Rapid Sketching and Observational Drawing
lessons.learningGoal: Apply rapid observational sketching techniques to represent proportional human figures and everyday ergonomic objects.

orientate.smartStart: In your workbook, sketch a continuous-line silhouette of your hand holding a pencil in 45 seconds without lifting your pencil.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can apply rapid sketching techniques to represent human proportions and everyday ergonomic tools

activities.title: Deconstructing Ergonomic Form (I Do)
activities.teacherDoes: Model on the whiteboard how designers deconstruct complex physical objects into primary geometric primitives (cylinders, cubes, prisms) using HB-4B pencils. Demonstrate establishing a primary bounding box, drawing the central longitudinal axis, and roughing in the hand-grip zone before refining line weights. Emphasise keeping construction lines faint so proportional adjustments can be made rapidly.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the step-by-step deconstruction on the board and replicate the three-part geometric breakdown of the everyday ergonomic tool in their workbook graphic workspace.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher deconstruction, then sketch the ergonomic tool breakdown including the 3 required elements: Bounding box, Central axis, and Hand-grip contact zone.
activities.questioning:
q: Why do designers construct faint geometric bounding boxes before adding curved surfaces?
Expected: Bounding boxes lock in height, width, and depth proportions early, preventing distorted perspective and asymmetric forms.
q: How does drawing a central axis help communicate ergonomic balance?
Expected: It establishes the structural core of the object, showing whether the grip aligns with the tool's line of action and force application.
activities.scaffolding: Demonstrated sequence: 1. Faint rectangular bounding prism (2H/HB pencil). 2. Centre axis line. 3. Tangent curves for finger recesses and grip contours. 4. Bold outline (2B pencil) on final contours.
activities.eLearning: Overhead document camera or whiteboard active for live drawing demonstration.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: now that we can deconstruct static tools, we will draw the human body that interacts with them.

workbookSpec.title: Ergonomic Tool Geometric Breakdown
workbookSpec.prompt: Construct the demonstrated ergonomic hand tool using rapid geometric blocking techniques.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Sketches must clearly show faint rectangular bounding box construction, a defined central longitudinal axis line, and an established ergonomic grip contour.

activities.workbookMaterials: Graphic sketching workspace with prompt requirements.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Sketches must exhibit: 1. Faint, visible geometric bounding box establishing correct tool proportions. 2. A clear centreline/axis showing tool balance. 3. Outlined ergonomic grip region demonstrating finger contour mapping.

activities.title: Proportional Figure Construction (We Do)
activities.teacherDoes: Co-construct a human figure in natural seated motion using the standard 7.5 to 8 head-height proportional system. Guide students head-by-head: mark Head Unit 1 at the top, mark Unit 4 at the pelvic baseline, and map articulated joint spheres at shoulders, elbows, hips, and knees. Show how drawing stick-and-joint gesture figures allows designers to rapidly evaluate reach zones and seating posture. Model the process clearly on the board before asking students to replicate it.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the step-by-step teacher cadence to construct an 8-head proportional figure seated at a desk, labelling head units, joint articulation points, and the posture spine curve directly in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Follow the teacher's pace on the grid to construct a proportional figure. Ensure you label: Head Unit 1, Pelvic baseline (Unit 4), and Joint articulation points.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is the 8-head proportional rule essential when drawing human figures in design contexts?
expected: It provides an accurate anatomical standard so designers do not design workspaces or furniture that are too large or too cramped for real humans.
q: What happens to posture when the pelvic baseline tilts backwards in a poorly designed chair?
expected: The lumbar spine collapses into a C-curve slump, increasing disc pressure and muscle strain.
activities.scaffolding: Workbook includes an 8-unit vertical scale with dashed guidelines for head height intervals: 1 = Head, 2 = Chest/Nipples, 3 = Navel/Waist, 4 = Pelvis/Groin, 5 = Mid-thigh, 6 = Knees, 7 = Mid-calf, 8 = Soles of feet.
activities.eLearning: Active circulation around student desks, inspecting pencil grip and vertical proportion alignment.
activities.transition: Transition from co-constructed human figures to independent observational tool annotation.

workbookSpec.title: Proportional Human Figure Workspace
workbookSpec.prompt: Construct a seated human figure demonstrating natural ergonomic interaction using the 8-head guideline system.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: A completed 7.5–8 head-height figure with clear cranial proportions, pelvic midpoint at Unit 4, spherical joint nodes, and dynamic natural posture.

activities.workbookMaterials: 8-head proportion guide grid and sketching workspace.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Figure must show: 1. Total height scaled accurately across 7.5 to 8 equal head units. 2. Torso and pelvic junction aligned at Unit 4. 3. Articulated joint spheres at shoulders, elbows, pelvis, and knees showing seated ergonomic interaction.

activities.title: Ergonomic Tool Callout Annotation (You Do)
activities.teacherDoes: Set up an observational display of an everyday ergonomic tool (e.g. heavy-duty utility cutter or hand stapler). Model on the board how professional industrial designers use crisp leader lines and numbered callouts to link visual product sketches to precise biomechanical justifications. For example, demonstrate drawing a clean line from a finger contour to a numbered box, stating: '1 is the grip contour because it reduces local contact pressure.' Direct students to work independently to sketch the displayed tool and complete the four technical callout descriptions in their workbooks.
activities.studentsDo: Independently sketch the displayed tool and write four structured callout annotations explaining how specific physical features reduce strain and accommodate human biomechanics.
activities.visibleInstructions: Sketch the displayed everyday tool and complete the 4 numbered callouts detailing how its design supports human grip, leverage, and comfort.
activities.questioning:
q: Why are numbered callouts preferred over messy text scribbled directly across a design sketch?
Expected: It keeps the technical drawing visually clean and readable while allowing detailed ergonomic justifications in an adjacent legend.
q: How does textured elastomeric material on a grip reduce user fatigue?
Expected: It increases friction, allowing the user to maintain secure control with significantly less hand squeeze pressure.
activities.scaffolding: Callout checklist prompts: Callout 1: Primary grip texture and friction point. Callout 2: Palm support curvature and pressure distribution. Callout 3: Finger placement contour or trigger recess. Callout 4: Mechanical leverage or force transmission axis.
activities.eLearning: Monitor individual workbooks from the perimeter of the room to ensure all students complete both sketch and callouts.
activities.transition: Direct students to set pencils down and prepare for partner review during Culminate.

workbookSpec.title: Ergonomic Hand Tool Technical Annotation
workbookSpec.prompt: Sketch the observed ergonomic tool and write 4 technical callout annotations explaining its physical human-centred features.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
1. Textured rubber overmould increases friction to prevent slippage during forceful pushes.
2. Arched palm rest distributes reaction forces across the thenar eminence to prevent localized pressure points.
3. Indented trigger channel cradles the index finger, providing positive tactile location without requiring visual check.
4. Offset handle angle aligns wrist with forearm in a neutral neutral position, mitigating repetitive strain injury.
workbookSpec.figureHint: Sketch the observed tool here, then draw neat leader lines to numbers 1–4 below.

activities.workbookMaterials: Annotated sketch figure workspace with 4 numbered callout blocks.
activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Grip texture: Elastomeric overmoulding to maximise friction and reduce required grip force.
2. Palm curvature: Broad contoured surface distributing load across palm.
3. Finger locator: Indented groove ensuring consistent finger placement away from pinch zones.
4. Force alignment: Handle angle maintains neutral wrist alignment during tool operation.

lessons.title: Evaluating Ergonomic Constraints and User Needs
lessons.learningGoal: Evaluate ergonomic design features by conducting a compliance audit, ranking user requirements, and rating physical constraints.

orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can evaluate ergonomic design features by auditing compliance, ranking user requirements, and justifying ratings

activities.title: Ergonomic Compliance Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the four key ergonomic pillars: Clearance, Reach, Posture, and Tactile Comfort, contextualising them within St Brendan's College classrooms and boarding facilities. Demonstrate how to audit a standard secondary school desk and chair setup using a formal checklist. Point out how rigid, non-adjustable furniture creates severe constraints for students at either extreme of the anthropometric spectrum (5th percentile vs 95th percentile).
activities.studentsDo: Conduct a physical audit of their immediate workstation against the 5 criteria in the workbook checklist, ticking met items and noting observable constraints.
activities.visibleInstructions: Audit your classroom chair and desk setup. Read each criterion in the checklist and tick the box if your workstation successfully meets that ergonomic standard.
activities.questioning:
What does anthropometric percentile mean in ergonomic design? Expected: It is the statistical distribution of human body dimensions across a population, typically designed to fit from the 5th to the 95th percentile.
Why is clearance space under a desk just as critical as seat height? Expected: Without adequate thigh and knee clearance, users cannot pull their chair close enough to write without hunching forward and twisting their spine.
activities.scaffolding: Key definitions provided on board: Anthropometrics: The comparative study of the measurements and capabilities of the human body. Ergonomics: Designing objects and environments to fit human biological limits. Lumbar support: Convex structural support that maintains the inward curve of the lower back.
activities.eLearning: Laptops down. Students stand and inspect desk-to-chair clearances and posture angles physically.
activities.transition: Pre-warn students: now that we have audited individual features, we must determine which user requirements are the highest priority.

workbookSpec.title: Classroom Workstation Ergonomic Compliance Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate your current St Brendan's College desk and chair against standard ergonomic criteria by ticking compliant items.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Criteria 1, 3, and 5 are typically compliant in modern secondary spaces; Criteria 2 (lumbar adjustment) and 4 (seat depth variation) frequently reveal design constraints.
items: Adjustable seat height or multiple shell sizes to support diverse anthropometric statures
Integrated lumbar contour that supports the natural inward lordotic curve of the spine
Unobstructed thigh and knee clearance allowing natural posture adjustments during sitting
Waterfall front edge on chair pan to prevent blood vessel and nerve compression under thighs
Desk work surface depth allows common tools to remain within the primary forearm reach zone

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Students evaluate their real chair/desk. Standard classroom furniture typically meets items 3 and 5, often meets 4, but rarely provides adjustable lumbar support (item 2) or seat height (item 1). Ticks must reflect real workstation observation.

activities.title: Prioritising User Requirements
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate how industrial designers balance conflicting stakeholder demands (e.g. low unit manufacturing cost vs premium ergonomic adjustability vs aesthetic styling). Walk through a priority ranking process, explaining why human physiological health and physical safety must take precedence over secondary aesthetic or decorative desires. Model your decision-making out loud: 'When I evaluate this furniture brief, safety and posture come before brand colours because physiological harm is irreversible while paint finishes are superficial.'
activities.studentsDo: Analyse the four scrambled user requirements in the workbook bank and order them into slots 1 to 4 from most critical to least critical for human-centred wellbeing.
activities.visibleInstructions: Rank the four user requirements from 1 (Most critical for user health and ergonomics) to 4 (Least critical) using the provided bank.
activities.questioning:
Why must spinal alignment and ergonomic support be prioritised over school branding colours in educational design? Expected: Inadequate spinal support can cause chronic musculoskeletal disorders and fatigue, directly impacting health and learning, whereas colours have no physical health impact.
Under what circumstances might material durability challenge ergonomic comfort? Expected: Highly rigid, indestructible plastics are cheap and durable for institutional use, but they provide poor pressure distribution and tactile comfort for users.
activities.scaffolding: Bank of items to order: Match institutional visual branding and aesthetic colours, Maintain spinal alignment and distribute body weight safely, Use durable, non-toxic, and easily cleanable materials, Provide adjustability for diverse anthropometric heights. Hint: Prioritise biomechanics first, durability second, aesthetics last.
activities.eLearning: Monitor student workbooks to check that rankings reflect reasoned design prioritisation rather than arbitrary guesses.
activities.transition: Direct students to transition from ranking high-level requirements to rating a specific everyday tool on a continuum.

activities.title: Ergonomic Effectiveness Rating
activities.teacherDoes: Model how to use a 1-to-5 continuum scale to rigorously evaluate an everyday tool (e.g. a standard non-cushioned metal ruler or a rigid plastic utility knife). Emphasise that assigning a score is meaningless without a technical justification referencing specific human factors (e.g. pinch grip strain, surface texture, pressure points). Model the sentence stem: 'This design rates a 2 on the continuum because the narrow, unyielding contact surface concentrates reaction forces directly onto the digital nerves of the thumb.'
activities.studentsDo: Select an everyday classroom tool, rate its ergonomic performance on the 1-to-5 continuum scale in the workbook, and write a three-line justification using precise ergonomic terminology.
activities.visibleInstructions: Mark your tool's rating on the 1-to-5 continuum, then complete the 3-line written justification addressing grip comfort, physical strain, and control.
activities.questioning:
What observable physical evidence justifies rating an object below 3 on the continuum? Expected: Evidence of sharp contact edges, slippery non-friction materials, excessive pinch force required, or unnatural joint deviation during use.
How does evaluating products on a continuum prevent black-and-white thinking in design analysis? Expected: It acknowledges that an object may have partial strengths (e.g., strong lever action) while possessing distinct ergonomic drawbacks (e.g., poor palm cushioning).
activities.scaffolding: Rating scale: 1 = Severe ergonomic flaws / high strain; 3 = Acceptable functional fit / minor fatigue; 5 = Exemplary human-centred fit / zero unnecessary strain. Sentence starter: 'This tool achieves an ergonomic rating of [X] because the [component] causes/prevents [physical constraint] during operation by...'
activities.eLearning: Rear-of-room monitoring, verifying that written justifications include at least two specific ergonomic vocabulary terms.
activities.transition: Guide students to close their workbooks after completing the justification and prepare for the Culminate phase.

workbookSpec.title: Everyday Tool Ergonomic Effectiveness Rating
workbookSpec.prompt: Rate the ergonomic effectiveness of the evaluated tool on the 1-to-5 scale, then justify your score based on user comfort and physical constraints.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Rating: 2 / 5. Justification: The unpadded rigid plastic casing forces a tight pinch grip with no thumb recess, causing localized muscle fatigue in the thenar eminence after short periods of repetitive cutting.

activities.workbookMaterials: Continuum scale rating bar with 3 lined justification rows.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Rating must be marked on the 1–5 scale. Written justification must explicitly mention: 1. A specific tool feature (grip surface, handle angle, edge radius). 2. The anatomical impact (wrist strain, finger friction, pressure concentration). 3. The functional outcome (user fatigue, reduced control).

culminate.smartFinish: Complete the 3-2-1 exit check on the final workbook line: 3 ergonomic factors audited today, 2 reasons why posture impacts learning, 1 question about designing for diverse human bodies.
culminate.summarise: Synthesised the week's foundational principles: auditing physical products against ergonomic criteria, prioritizing human biomechanical needs, and rating usability constraints.

What are the negative long-term impacts of total ground clearing during housing estate development? Expected: Loss of topsoil, complete disruption of wildlife corridors, destruction of cultural heritage, and microclimate heating.

activities.title: Annotation Conventions and Standards
activities.teacherDoes: Model the technical conventions of formal design annotations under the document camera. Demonstrate: 1. Ruling straight leader lines with a 15-centimetre ruler that terminate with a precise dot or arrowhead on the specific feature. 2. Aligning all explanatory text horizontally in neat architectural lettering. 3. Formulating an impact annotation using the 'Feature + Function + Impact' formula (e.g., 'Perforated recycled aluminium louvres -> filters harsh western sun -> reduces radiant heat stress for community elders'). Contrast this against weak, non-analytical labels like 'Metal roof'.

activities.questioning:
Why are horizontal leader lines and uncrossed callouts mandatory in technical communication? Expected: Crossed or diagonal multi-angle text creates visual clutter and leads to manufacturing misinterpretation or reader confusion.

activities.scaffolding:

activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the three mandatory exam analysis terms: Design Constraint, User Perspective, and Cultural Context. Model identifying each term within a sample brief excerpt on the whiteboard: 'Notice the phrase "budget capped at $5,000 using marine-grade recycled timber"; this is an explicit material and financial constraint. activities.questioning:
q: Why are constraints essential rather than limiting in a design exam?

activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:

2. User Perspective: The lived experience, physical requirements, and emotional needs of the specific person interacting with the solution.
3. Cultural Context: The social, historical, and environmental connection to Country and local community identity that informs ethical design.

For example: 'Callout 1 points to the slatted timber canopy: "Marine-grade spotted gum slats angled at 35 degrees to block midday tropical UV while allowing sea breeze cross-ventilation, meeting user shade needs and coastal durability constraints."' Expected: It might deliver community utility while simultaneously violating intellectual property, misusing cultural narratives, or excluding key community groups from decision-making.

activities.title: Modelling Critique, Justify, and Refine
activities.teacherDoes: Project an unrefined sample design concept (a coastal public wayfinding kiosk for Keppel Bay Marina) onto the board. Model the 3-stage iterative cycle: 1. Critique (Identify flaws: high visual clutter, lack of shaded resting areas, unverified cultural motifs). 2. Justify (Reference exam criteria: poor ergonomic accessibility for elderly tourists, failure to align with Darumbal storytelling protocols). 3. Refine (Model redrafting: separate signage into high-contrast visual zones, add tactile paving, integrate approved historical narrative panels). Record these three steps live on the board.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's critique sequence. Transcribe the modelled gap, justification, and refinement action into the structured sections of your workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Record the three modelled steps (Critique, Justify, Refine) in your workbook to document how design flaws are converted into validated improvements.
activities.questioning: How does articulating a justification prevent arbitrary styling decisions? Expected: It forces the designer to anchor modifications to concrete user needs, cultural integrity, or rubric standards rather than subjective personal taste. Why must the initial draft flaw remain visible alongside the refined version? Expected: It provides an audit trail that demonstrates deliberate, reflective problem-solving to the examiner.
activities.scaffolding:
Iterative Protocol:
- Critique: State the specific failure in usability, accessibility, or cultural alignment.
- Justify: Connect the failure directly to rubric criteria (Social Impact, Cultural Significance, Ethics).
- Refine: Formulate an actionable modification to overcome the deficiency.

activities.title: Part A Task 2: Grounded Empathy Mapping
activities.teacherDoes:
Maintain examination discipline while providing guided pacing cues. Prompt: 'Ensure each quadrant is grounded in explicit evidence from the brief. The Feels quadrant must capture deep emotional states such as feeling disconnected, overwhelmed, or eager to learn, rather than simple physical actions.' Monitor student progress against the required 4-quadrant format.
Modelled Example:
Teacher: Notice how the 'Says' quadrant relies on verbatim quotation marks directly lifting text from the persona brief. For 'Thinks', we infer the cognitive state behind those words—what the user holds as internal beliefs or worries.
activities.studentsDo: Extract qualitative statements, observed actions, cognitive thoughts, and emotional feelings from the user persona provided in the exam brief. Record evidence-based responses into the four rows of your workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Populate the four quadrants of the Empathy Map table using direct evidence and inferences drawn from the exam persona narrative under strict examination conditions.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the critical distinction between what a persona 'Says' and what they 'Feel'?
expected: 'Says' records explicit verbal comments, whereas 'Feels' infers the deeper emotional frustration, vulnerability, or joy beneath those words.
question: Why is it essential that empathy data reflects cultural context?
expected: It prevents cultural assumptions and ensures the solution honors community lived experience and traditional custodian perspectives.
activities.scaffolding:
Empathy Map Dimensions:
- Says: Direct quotes regarding navigation difficulties, cultural curiosity, or project requirements.
- Thinks: Beliefs about safety, environmental respect, and site accessibility.
- Does: Observed behaviours such as checking smartphones, hesitating at unmarked junctions, or consulting local maps.
- Feels: Feelings of confusion, exclusion, respect, or desire for belonging.

activities.transition: Pre-warn students at 14 minutes: 'Ensure all four quadrants contain evidence. Moving to Task 3: Ethical Design Protocols.'

activities.questioning:
Why are 3D projection techniques preferred over flat 2D elevations when presenting design proposals to community stakeholders? Expected: They communicate volumetric scale, spatial relationships, and aesthetic form clearly to non-technical audiences.
How does line weight variation improve technical communication in concept sketches? Expected: Heavy boundary outlines establish silhouette and depth, while fine interior lines show surface transitions and construction details.
activities.scaffolding:
Drafting Standards:
- Proportion and geometric layout (30-degree isometric axis or 2-point perspective)
- Linework hierarchy: Light construction lines -> Medium feature lines -> Dark silhouette outlines
- Visual representation of physical accessibility (e.g., wheelchair clearances, tactile indicators, shade canopy)

activities.title: Part B Task 2: Triple-Layered Annotation Execution
activities.teacherDoes: Provide a structured pacing checkpoint for formal annotation under QCAA examination conditions. Deliver this explicit instruction: 'Every callout must follow our mandatory three-part structure: Component Name -> Technical Function -> User/Cultural Justification. A callout that only states what an item is cannot achieve above a C standard.' Model an exemplary annotation on the whiteboard for a coastal shade structure: '1. Cantilevered Aluminium Louvres -> Regulates solar radiation heat gain while directing prevailing sea breezes -> Directly addresses user feedback regarding thermal comfort while respecting local environmental constraints.' Supervise as students add four critical annotations to their drawing.
activities.studentsDo: Rule four leader lines from specific features on your concept sketch to the annotation ledger. Write complete three-part annotations explaining component name, technical function, and ethical or cultural justification.
activities.visibleInstructions: Add four numbered annotations to your sketch using the formula: [Component Name] -> [Technical Function] -> [Cultural/User Justification].
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why must every technical annotation include a cultural or user justification?
expected: It demonstrates that each physical element directly answers an identified user need or respects ethical guidelines rather than being purely decorative.
prompt: What is the purpose of using ruled leader lines with distinct touchpoints?
expected: To maintain engineering drawing clarity and eliminate ambiguity about which specific feature is being described.
activities.scaffolding:
Annotation Formula:
1. Component: Name of material, mechanism, or form
2. Function: What it does physically, ergonomically, or environmentally
3. Justification: Why it meets user needs, enhances accessibility, or respects Darumbal culture
activities.eLearning: None.
